Making a Better Battery Credit: Raw Pixel/Pixabay Helping smartphones hold their charge longer. Light-weight and energy-efficient, lithium-ion batteries have long been the battery of choice for powering smartphones, laptops, hoverboards, drones and other portable electronic devices. But even these low-maintenance batteries have their drawbacks—they lose their ability to hold charge after about 3 years, can catch on fire and often have to be recharged daily. To make a better lithium-ion battery or find innovative alternatives, PML researchers in collaboration with scientists from the Material Measurement Laboratory (MML) are studying how lithium batteries behave on some of the tiniest of scales, a few tens of atoms across. The scientists use an instrument that injects with exquisite precision an ultranarrow beam of lithium ions (charged atoms of lithium) into the negative terminal of a laboratory battery. pages.text: Mammals Made By Viruses | National Geographic SCIENCE THE LOOM Mammals Made By Viruses By Carl Zimmer Published February 14, 2012 • 6 min read If not for a virus, none of us would ever be born. In 2000, a team of Boston scientists discovered a peculiar gene in the human genome. It encoded a protein made only by cells in the placenta. They called it syncytin. The cells that made syncytin were located only where the placenta made contact with the uterus. They fuse together to create a single cellular layer, called the syncytiotrophoblast, which is essential to a fetus for drawing nutrients from its mother. The scientists discovered that in order to fuse together, the cells must first make syncytin. What made syncytin peculiar was that it was not a human gene. It bore all the hallmarks of a gene from a virus. Viruses have insinuated themselves into the genome of our ancestors for hundreds of millions of years. They typically have gotten there by infecting eggs or sperm, inserting their own DNA into ours. There are 100,000 known fragments of viruses in the human genome, making up over 8% of our DNA. Most of this virus DNA has been hit by so many mutations that it’s nothing but baggage our species carries along from one generation to the next. Yet there are some viral genes that still make proteins in our bodies. Syncytin appeared to be a hugely important one to our own biology. City have appealed, with a sanction yet to be decided. The club's sponsors Etihad and Etisalat have both said they are considering legal action against the Premier League. But the league's rules will now be amended to provide legal indemnity for CEO Richard Masters, chair Alison Brittan and three other non-executive directors. Sources have told BBC Sport that City were one of two Premier League clubs that voted against the amendment, with the other 18 clubs voting in favour. An independent commission appointed by the Premier League found City guilty of artificially inflating the club's revenues by over £830m over a nine-year period in September. The commission determined that the club arranged "sham" contracts with sponsors, which disguised funding from club owners the Abu Dhabi United Group. Premier League CEO Masters said City "systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade". Treasures of the Globally Popular Japanese Comic Book Medium Are on View in New York Skip to main content The first rooms of the "Art of Manga" exhibition introduce visitors to manga, which is read right-to-left and usually published in black and white. Paula Abreu Pita Manga are Japanese comic books and graphic novels. They are typically written and illustrated by a single person, known as mangaka . They are usually printed in black and white and read right-to-left. And they are incredibly popular, in Japan and beyond. When Frederik L. Schodt, author of Manga! Manga! The World of Japanese Comics , published his book in the 1980s, “almost no one in the United States knew what manga was,” he tells the New York Times ’ Shivani Vora. Things have changed. Manga’s popularity is booming in the United States. “Today, young Americans have no problem with manga at all,” he says. “They are happy to read them Japanese-style, turning pages and viewing panels right-to-left.” More than 40 percent of Gen Z watches anime shows, which are often adaptations of manga, compared to just 25 percent who follow professional football. Now, the illustrated medium and its most well-known mangaka are the centerpiece of a new exhibition at the Brooklyn Museum in New York. “ Art of Manga ” is the country’s first large-scale show to explore the art form’s evolution, individual voices and cross-cultural impact. “The show’s focus on artists is what makes it so special. As reported by the Bureau of Economic Analysis , manufacturing accounted for 31.4 % of U.S. research and development value added. In terms of total economic value added, the U.S. is the second largest manufacturing country in the world. Promoting innovation and industrial competitiveness in manufacturing can often require understanding the economics of the industry. Combined, these serve as a resource for research in robotics for advanced manufacturing and material handling. The test bed contains representative state-of-the-art manufacturing robots, including ones that have been designed specifically for safe interactions with human workers in shared environments. The testbed also includes advanced multi-fingered grippers, sensors, conveyors, and an industrial robot arm that can be mounted on a linear rail or on a pedestal. A custom-configured automatic guided vehicle (AGV) is used for research in industrial vehicle safety and performance standards, including mobile manipulation. The robot systems also include vision and force-torque sensing capability. During those days, I discovered it was so much more: a regional community, with faces, stories, perspectives, and generosity. I understood why these in-person gatherings matter so much. Enlarge this image Doby/NPR Doby/NPR Mara Liasson Correspondent, Washington Desk Mara Liasson is the senior national political correspondent for NPR. Her reports can be heard regularly on NPR's award-winning newsmagazine programs Morning Edition and All Things Considered . Liasson provides extensive coverage of politics and policy from Washington, DC — focusing on the White House and Congress — and also reports on political trends beyond the Beltway. Each election year, Liasson provides key coverage of the candidates and issues in both presidential and congressional races. During her tenure she has covered nine presidential elections — in 1992, 1996, 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020, and 2024. Prior to her current assignment, Liasson was NPR's White House correspondent for all eight years of the Clinton administration. She has won the White House Correspondents' Association's Merriman Smith Award for daily news coverage in 1994, 1995, and again in 1997. From 1989-1992 Liasson was NPR's congressional correspondent. Liasson joined NPR in 1985 as a general assignment reporter and newscaster. From September 1988 to June 1989 she took a leave of absence from NPR to attend Columbia University in New York as a recipient of a Knight-Bagehot Fellowship in Economics and Business Journalism. Marcos Gonzales Harsha Marcos serves as the Principal Deputy Director at the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE's) Office of Technology Commercialization (OTC). In conjunction with the Director, Marcos works with program offices within DOE as well as with the national labs to identify and increase awareness of partnership opportunities for the private sector to access and leverage DOE's portfolio of pioneering R&D, leading scientists and experts, and world-class facilities. Prior to joining OTC in November 2017, he served in roles of increasing responsibility in the Office of the Under Secretary for Science and Energy (now Under Secretary for Science), starting in 2013 as a budget advisor and departing as the Deputy Chief of Staff. During his time with the Under Secretary's Office, Marcos led an effort to stand up six interdisciplinary crosscutting teams covering topics ranging from the energy-water nexus to grid modernization with a budget footprint of nearly $1 billion of DOE’s R&D portfolio. In his capacity with the Under Secretary, Marcos also helped to stand up both the Office of Technology Transitions and the Energy Investor Center. pages.text: Marcus Street: Saracens prop signs new two-year deal - BBC Sport Image source, Shutterstock Image caption, Marcus Street spent eight years with Exeter Chiefs before joining Saracens in 2025 Published 4 hours ago Saracens tighthead prop Marcus Street has signed a new two-year contract with the club. The 27-year-old has established himself as a key player in the forward pack since arriving from Exeter Chiefs in March 2025. Street has started four of five Prem games this season for Sarries, who are fourth in the table. He also made 22 appearances in all competitions in the 2025-26 campaign - his first with the north London club. "I want to give thanks to the club, the coaches and the fans for giving me the opportunity to grow as a player and more," said Street, who also helps coach scrums and set pieces with the Saracens women's team. "I'm grateful for the chance to re-sign and continue that." Saracens head coach Joe Shaw said he was "delighted" Street had committed his immediate future to the club. "He brings real strength and quality to our set piece and it's been fantastic to see how quickly he's become such an integral part of the group, both on and off the field," Shaw told the club website. , external "His commitment to the club has been clear from day one, and we're really pleased to have him on board for the next chapter." Credit: M. King/NIST I previously wrote a blog post about Ada Lovelace , often celebrated as “the world’s first computer programmer.” While I genuinely enjoyed crafting that piece, I wished for the opportunity to write about a scientist who is much closer to my heart: Maria Skłodowska-Curie. She has always been and remains a personal role model. Maria Skłodowska-Curie (commonly known as Marie Curie) revolutionized our understanding of the atomic world. Her work had profound, long-lasting effects on medicine, technology and the course of human history. Growing up and going to school in Poland, I learned about Curie early on in an elementary school science course. I also remember seeing her pictures in every physics and chemistry classroom.

pages.text: Mario Balotelli: Why always him? The rise and fall of the Italian striker - BBC Sport By Jess Anderson BBC Sport journalist Maverick. Loose cannon. Unmanageable. Mario Balotelli heard it all. Perhaps better known for off-field antics than his undeniable - yet arguably wasted - talent with the ball at his feet, the Italian has always attracted headlines. Fifteen years have passed since his famous 'Why always me?' Manchester derby T-shirt celebration, which came just days after a firework was set off in his own bathroom, causing a house fire. The 36-year-old is still playing, now in the United Arab Emirates first division with Al-Ittifaq alongside his biological brother, Enock Barwuah. Here, BBC Sport looks at a career that has included 13 clubs, six countries - and an assist for arguably the most famous goal in Premier League history. Mancini to Mourinho - cracks begin to show Typical of his unconventional footballing life, Balotelli's career did not begin in an elite club's academy. Instead, by his mid-teens he was turning out for Italian third-tier side Lumezzane, close to the family home in Concesio. A trial at Barcelona did not lead to a long-term stay, and instead he was picked up by Inter Milan in 2006. It was at Inter that Balotelli first came across his great mentor - Roberto Mancini. The relationship between the two has been likened to that of a father and son. Under the Italian coach's tutelage, Balotelli flourished. pages.text: Mario Batali on Why Farmers Should Be the True Stars of the Restaurant World Skip to main content Quentin Bacon The premise of a chef becoming a world-famous figure is a recent phenomenon, with multiple television networks airing their own versions of reality cooking shows and competitive culinary battles. But if chef-lebrity Mario Batali has his way, the farmer, a person critical to the creation of the meal on your plate, will take over center stage. In his new book, America—Farm to Table , Mario Batali shifts the spotlight: “where chefs once ruled the waves, local small farmers are the new rock stars.” The famous restaurateur and chef teamed up with Washington Post writer Jim Webster to capture the stories of a select group of farmers from across the country and create recipes from their specialty ingredients. To gain access to these deserving future celebrities, Batali looked to his chef friends from Maine to California. He asked chefs from Jose Andres in Washington D.C. to Matt Dillon in Seattle which growers they depend on for their most beloved ingredients; the taste and freshness of the ingredients are just as important to the final plate as the culinary art. Mariza Smajlaj Mariza Smajlaj Mariza Smajlaj is the Director of Communications for NNSA, where she leads strategic communications and public engagement for one of the nation's most critical missions: safeguarding national security through the responsible stewardship of nuclear weapons technology. With a background in communications, policy, and advocacy, she translates complex initiatives into accessible information. Before joining NNSA, Ms. Smajlaj was the Communications Director at a social impact public affairs firm, where she managed campaigns on pressing societal issues. She also served as Communications Director for a U.S. House Foreign Affairs Committee member, shaping messaging on global security. Her media experience spans multiple perspectives, from working as an associate producer at Sinclair Broadcast Group to serving as the editor at theSkimm, where she distilled policy topics for broad audiences. Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images US military This article is more than 10 months old Mark Kelly sues Hegseth over ‘chilling’ effort to reduce military retirement rank This article is more than 10 months old US defense secretary Pete Hegseth tried to reduce veteran’s pension for speaking out against Trump administration Richard Luscombe Mon 12 Jan 2026 15.14 EST Last modified on Mon 12 Jan 2026 15.22 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Democratic US senator Mark Kelly filed a lawsuit on Monday seeking to nullify the “chilling” attempt by the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, to reduce the military veteran’s rank and pension as punishment for speaking out against the Trump administration . pages.text: Marriage/Domestic Partnership | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Marriage/Domestic Partnership When you get married, you can change your health coverage. You can add yourself, your new spouse and children to your employer’s plan, enroll in your spouse’s employer’s plan, or find coverage through the Health Insurance Marketplace (Marketplace). Get the details on all of your special enrollment options and be sure you understand how the different plans work. You'll want to know the benefits covered, the amounts of any deductibles or copays you will be required to pay, what you will pay for premiums, and whether you can continue with the same doctors. For your retirement plan, when there is a change in your personal information, such as marriage, contact your plan administrator or the human resources department to change your status under the plan and provide them with updated contact information for you. Getting married also creates new financial demands that compete for retirement dollars, such as changing life insurance needs and saving to buy a home. But it's usually less expensive for two people to live together, thus freeing up dollars. A spending plan is essential. Photograph by Tommy Trenchard, Panos Pictures/Redux By Cathy Newman Published March 29, 2021 • 11 min read If you had lived in Victorian times, you’d have spotted her, perhaps, at the foot of Church Cliff to the east of Lyme Regis, a seaside town on England’s southwest coast. She’d have a wicker basket in one hand, a small geologist’s hammer in the other, and be dressed in a plaid coat and cape made of heavy wool—it is chilly by the shore. Her small dog, Tray, would have been skittering by her side. Self-taught paleontologist Mary Anning would search for fossils along the Dorset coast, accompanied by her dog, Tray. A team of researchers took this approach when studying the fabric masks that people wear to slow the spread of COVID-19. Those masks work by blocking some of the virus-filled droplets and smaller particles, called aerosols, that an infected person exhales, and they also offer some protection to the wearer by filtering incoming air. The researchers wanted to know how well different fabrics filter out those particles and what makes some fabrics better filters than others. Their research indicates that that cotton fabrics tend to perform better than synthetics , with cotton flannels being particularly effective.
